recommendedPopulationClaim.text: Smith and colleagues propose approximately 100,000 residents for Xolalpan–Metepec Teotihuacan using a reanalysis of mapped residences and excavated dwellings.
recommendedPopulationClaim.locator: Abstract; Population Estimates; Table 5; Discussion and Conclusions
recommendedPopulationClaim.limitations: Published estimate can be quoted; no new persons-per-room conversion is performed. Household size, contemporaneity and housing classifications remain assumptions. Millon 1970 gave a probable 125,000, with a minimum 75,000 and possible more than 200,000; that open upper alternative must not be turned into a finite max. These are rival models, not population change.

updates.reasonNoSeries: No bounded CE span for the preferred Xolalpan–Metepec reconstruction was independently extracted from this article. A circa 60,000 estimate at 100 CE in Cowgill’s chapter summary suggests growth but is a different model and does not establish a consistent dated series.

updates.locationAssessment: The existing UNESCO point is the public reference of the 38,160.87 ha sanctuary, not an exact coordinate of the llaqta’s occupied urban core. Keep its honest sanctuary label until a verified city-specific institutional GIS point is acquired.
updates.reasonNoSeries: The 2021 burial-dating study supports occupation chronology, not a resident headcount. Do not translate dated individuals, buildings, or modern visitors into population.

updates.locationAssessment: A point at Templo Mayor can locate that actual complex; it cannot silently stand for Tlatelolco or the full conurbation. The new site record is separate.
updates.reasonNoSeries: Ortman et al.’s approximately 200,000 is not a source-supported 1200–1519 CE constant. Their analytical cohort does not date the city’s population estimate at every year. No bounded series is recommended.

unresolved.issue: Dated change is demonstrated using a published reconstruction reproduced by an official museum. The primary 1997 chapter was not directly accessible. Do not present the values as a new census or a securely verified original numerical table.

Acquire a public city-specific point from Ministry of Culture GIS or a georeferenced archaeological publication; the UNESCO sanctuary reference is too broad to claim exact urban location. No verified resident estimate found in the consulted chronology source.

Joyce and Henderson 2001 names the excavated site. Its open-ended pre-1600 BCE onset remains unplaced; the 1100–900 BCE exchange episode is bounded. Use the archaeological CR-372 locality, not the unrelated same-name gazetteer town at 15.466667, -86.5.

These are specific excavated places hidden behind regional-evidence titles. The existing source-specific episodes can become separate point records when public archaeological coordinates are verified. Do not substitute a regional anchor or a same-name modern municipality. Aguada Fénix construction is 1000–800 BCE, not the whole settlement span.

Chamical has a 1410–1480 cal CE onset model ready to link to a verified public archaeological point. Ak’awillay, Yanawilka and Guitián need bounded local episodes before becoming dated settlement records. Do not use Cuzco, Vilcas Huamán or North Calchaquí regional anchors as exact site points.

Extract each named site, its local occupation evidence and its own public location from original tables/maps. Regional onset models, 1500 pottery-positive sites, 40 inventory settlements and valley-wide intervention stages do not supply identical dates or city populations for each constituent place.

sites: TYYS sampled context (Tatóok yík yées sháawat), distinct from Shuká Káa
unresolved.issue: Distinguish sampled individuals, a named archaeological locality and complexes containing many sites. Extract publication-specific dates for each occupation. Genomic continuity, regional environments, houses and summed radiocarbon distributions are not resident headcounts. Do not expose burial coordinates as if they were public settlement centroids.

Regional earliest-occupation posterior estimates and Ceramic-related ancestry models do not establish every site’s founding, identity or population. Extract named sites and public localities from chronology tables; genetic effective size and sampled kin numbers must not resize resident dots.

Tikal already has a site record; avoid duplicating it as another generic city. Its Corriental row uses a park reference, not the reservoir. Retain the dated sediment scope and refine only from the primary reservoir map. Tomb 105 is a context, not a whole-city occupation or resident estimate.

Keep the same actual site identity across occupation and exchange records. Do not treat multiple copper geological sources as new occupied cities or transport routes; ceremonial monuments do not automatically imply permanent resident estimates.

Park-level and regional-center records should be followed by independently named, dated public settlements where original source tables permit. Use Hovenweep’s individually supported sites as the pattern, while retaining region-level syntheses separately. Do not turn room totals into people.

These already identify actual dated contexts. A public site locator should remain distinct from exact excavation/sample coordinates, regional centroid, or complete occupation. No resident estimate should be inferred from artifact counts or dated specimens.
